notes.1a: Well answered as most candidates showed some understanding of the term by being able to identify one relevant feature. The best responses recognised that it involved sole ownership of a business.
notes.1b: Well answered as most candidates were able to identify at least one measure of success. Typical answers included profit and increased market share. A common mistake was to simply state words like ‘assets’ or ‘output’ without clarifying how these might be measures of success.
notes.1c: Most candidates could identify at least two relevant methods of communication. The best responses developed the points to show how these methods would help Rafa and his managers communicate with each other. There were three common mistakes: some candidates simply reworded the knowledge points identified rather than offering any explanation, others attempted to explain the information that would be communicated rather than the benefits of using such methods and a few candidates stated generic advantages such as cheaper or faster, without identifying either a method or explaining how it would be cheaper or faster.
notes.1d: Answers here were often good. Many candidates were able to identify and explain three appropriate management functions. Some candidates focused solely on the management of workers, often repeating the same point rather than identifying different functions, which restricted the number of marks they could access. The same point can only be credited once. Others ignored the context and identified points that were not appropriate to a shop manager.
notes.1e: This question differentiated very effectively across the ability range. There were a number of good answers to this question. Most candidates could identify a range of possible issues, both for and against, opening more shops. Weaker candidates did not always support the knowledge shown with appropriate analysis linking more shops to the possible impact on profitability. Better candidates were able to develop these points and use this analysis to support their final recommendation. Evaluation in many responses was simple or not attempted. It should be noted that a simple ‘yes’ or ‘no’ does not constitute evaluation on its own, but should follow on from the argument built up in their answer. The question requires a recommendation and, a failure to provide one, restricts the number of marks that a candidate’s answer can gain. It did not matter which way the candidate concluded.
notes.2a: This question produced a mixture of responses. The best answers recognised both the ownership and short-term nature of current assets. Others were able to identify one of these elements and support their definition with an appropriate example. The common mistake was to simply repeat the term ‘asset’, which was stated in the stem, without explaining what the word meant. Candidates need to be encouraged to provide greater accuracy when defining terms.
notes.2b: There were many correct answers seen. Common errors were to express the answer as a % or use the figures for the wrong year. Where candidates had included the correct formula, the responses could still achieve one mark. It is very important that candidates always include the relevant formula for all calculation questions.
notes.2c: This question proved challenging for many candidates. Better candidates were able to identify and explain situations where an overdraft might be used. Some candidates assumed that an overdraft could be used in any business purpose, so offered suggestions such as purchasing fixed assets. As an overdraft is only used for short term business needs, such answers were clearly incorrect and could not be rewarded.
notes.2d: Most candidates were able to identify at least two changes in the data. Better candidates were able to develop the points. A common mistake was to simply repeat the knowledge mark rather than explain why the changes might have occurred. Few candidates attempted any quantitative analysis of the data.
notes.2e: This question differentiated clearly between candidates. Most candidates were able to identify what the accounts might show to different stakeholders. Better candidates explained how the stakeholder might use this information. The best candidates considered how useful this information might be for each stakeholder, so earning evaluation marks. Weaker answers focused on ‘the accounts’ rather than highlighting the elements of the accounts which different stakeholders might be interested in, such as profit or level of debt. Some candidates did not identify any stakeholders. This led to generalised answers which could not be rewarded.
notes.3a: This question proved challenging for many candidates. Better candidates were able to provide a precise definition of a niche market. Some candidates understood that it was a market with ‘specific’ characteristics. Many incorrectly assumed that it was just a ‘small market’, which did not sufficiently explain the term. Candidates must try to be more precise when providing definitions of key terms.
notes.3b: Most candidates were able to identify appropriate ways to segment a market with gender and income being popular responses.
notes.3c: Most candidates were able to identify relevant reasons with ‘out of date’ and ‘inaccuracy’ being common choices. Better responses developed the points to show why the information collected might be of limited value to a business. A common mistake was to repeat the same knowledge point for both reasons. Others identified two reasons but simply reworded the knowledge point in their explanation. Either type of response will only be credited once.
notes.3d: Generally well answered as most candidates were able to identify at least two reasons why a business might spend money on advertising. Better responses developed these points. Weaker candidates tended to repeat the knowledge point rather than explain why the spending was necessary. A few candidates repeated the same knowledge point for more than one reason.
notes.3e: This question produced a good range of answers. Most candidates were able to list a number of points both for and against offering cheaper holidays. Better candidates were able to develop these points to explain the possible impact on Koni Travel. It was pleasing to see that many candidates recognised the fact that they operated in a niche market and explored points in this context. The best responses incorporated this fact into their analysis to help them reach a logical decision based on the context of this business.
notes.4a: The majority of candidates had some understanding of flow production as they knew it referred to ‘high volume’ production. Better candidates were able to either provide a precise definition or identify two distinctive features. Some candidates who simply defined what production was rather than flow production, did not answer the question set. It is important that candidates read the question carefully. Others described batch production which was clearly incorrect.
notes.4b: Generally well answered by most candidates. The most common mistake was to assume that profit is a measure of size.
notes.4c: Many candidates recognised reasons such as efficiency or motivation of the workers. Better responses were able to develop the reasons to explain how the information might help management. A common mistake was to offer generalised statements such as ‘help make decisions’ without explaining how knowing the ‘output per employee’ could be helpful.
notes.4d: This question proved challenging for many candidates. A number of candidates had the wrong focus and assumed that a high labour turnover was a measure of high productivity. Their answers incorrectly explained points such as ‘being well trained’ or ‘workers are highly motivated’. Others assumed turnover referred to increased production and considered why output might have increased. Neither approach was credited. Better responses identified relevant reasons such as ‘lack of motivation’ or ‘poor working conditions’ and attempted to explain why these issues might lead to people leaving the business. The best responses linked these points to a manufacturing business, which was what the question required.
notes.4e: Most candidates were able to identify possible economies or diseconomies of scale. Better responses did attempt to analyse the points and make reasoned judgements that recognised that unit costs were only likely to fall up to a point. Weaker candidates tended to list points but were not able to explain how or why these points might need to be considered. Evaluation in many responses was simple or not attempted.
notes.5a: This question produced a mixture of responses. Many candidates knew that it was someone who took ‘risks’. Better candidates provided a precise definition. A common misunderstanding was to assume that an entrepreneur was a sole trader and so define this term rather than the one asked for in the question.
notes.5b: Well answered by virtually all candidates.
notes.5c: Most candidates were able to identify two relevant features of an employment contract. Better candidates were able to explain the features. There were two common mistakes: some candidates confused the term with either a job description or job specification and others offered analysis that was a repetition of the knowledge point, rather than an explanation.
notes.5d: Good knowledge of ways that laws safeguard workers was evident in most responses. Most candidates were aware of issues such as protection against unfair dismissal, minimum wages and safer working conditions. Better candidates were able to develop all these points to show how the workers were protected.
notes.5e: This question proved to be a good discriminator. To score highly on this question, candidates needed to explain how businesses, and in particular the amount of profit made, might be affected by the laws. Most candidates were able to outline at least one relevant issue. Typical answers focused on costs of training or safety equipment. Weaker candidates were not able to explain why these points should affect the business. Some simply suggested that it might affect ‘profit’ without explaining how or why this might occur. Better candidates made this link and tried to make a reasoned judgment as to whether profits would be affected or not. A number of candidates had the wrong focus as they only considered the effects on employees, not on the business. Evaluation in many responses was simple or not attempted.
notes.key_messages:
• Questions requiring simple answers were generally well done, but greater precision is needed in the
use of business terminology.
• Candidates must consider the context when answering individual questions.
• Answers to part (c) and (d) questions require candidates to identify and explain points. To gain full
marks, development of each point identified is required.
• Part (e) questions should include developed points and a logical decision based on the points made.
notes.general_comments:
The paper discriminated well between candidates of differing abilities. The range of marks was between 97
and low single figures. This spread was broadly in line with the performance of candidates in previous
sessions.
Many candidates demonstrated good knowledge and understanding of the relevant concepts. It was
encouraging to see that virtually all candidates attempted each question. Candidates performed particularly
well on concepts such as types of organisation, communication and implications of government laws. There
was clear evidence of some parts of the syllabus not being understood by candidates, for example concepts
such as labour turnover and unit costs. It is important for candidates to know that they can be assessed on
any aspect of the syllabus.
Candidates were clear about what was required for each question, and most attempted to provide some
analysis of points made. However when asked to explain points, candidates must ensure they develop the
original point rather than simply repeating the same point or identifying another knowledge point.
Parts (e) of all questions are the most challenging for candidates. These questions require candidates to
demonstrate both analysis and evaluative skills. Lists of knowledge points alone can only gain a maximum
of two marks. Evaluation marks cannot be awarded if candidates do not make a decision at all or if the
decision made is not linked to the knowledge and analysis points made.
